paragraphs.text: By ancestral law and an ancient custom, which sons have received from their forebears and keep to this day, the Roman soldiers put on their full armour at the beginning of the present month. They go out to a plain that is wide and level enough to stage a horse race, practise tactics and train in every kind of armed exercise, and there they mark the new year and keep the day as a festival. I, for my part, am celebrating the memory of martyrs, as I announced to you yesterday. Today, by this commemoration, I arm the forty soldiers of Christ, who outdid all zeal in their contests, and I set them forth as a marvel for those able to see: the adornment of the Church, the joy of the peoples, and the glory of God who strengthened them. It is surely best, and very profitable, for the young to be nourished on stories of virtue, and for grown men to flourish together with them. Hearing is the most vital of the senses, and it teaches no less than sight, for through the ears it brings learning vividly into souls. So there is no small risk in whether the stories we hear are good or bad. Whatever they are like when they are told, an image of the same kind must arise in our thoughts, and the mind's reflection and constant contemplation lead a person to desire to do what he thinks about. So prepare for me a calm and undistracted hearing, that the blessed martyrs may be honoured as is fitting, and that you through their commemoration may be taught piety and [?]
Before me lies a twofold contest, and I fear that I may insult my subject by the weakness of my telling. Whether one considers the grandeur of the matter in hand itself, it

carries off the prize against all speech. Or one considers him who before us crowned the saints by his own wisdom: a man whom the whole world alike admires; an exact rule of learning, both Christian and secular; an image of philosophy; a pattern and [?] for bishops; a teacher whose deeds agree with his words. Among all people he enjoys a reputation without rival, except among those for whom not even Christ is spared blasphemy. As no one disputes that the sun gives light and warmth, so no one will deny that the great Basil was adorned with every beauty of virtue. Lofty himself, he praised the lofty; holy himself, he served the holy; and with the power that was in him he paid the champions their prize in full. Yet I need not keep silent because the one who went before me proclaimed these wonders so grandly. My aim now is not to compete with him who has spoken, but to care for the benefit of you who listen. Each person surely helps as much as he can, while the richer supply the enjoyment of greater things.

The forty, then, were soldiers. Their station in life had given them service under arms to the emperor of the Romans, but by faith they were Christians and in religion they were devout. The ruler of that time was one of those who worship many gods, and the demons suggested to him that bitter plan. By a new law and edict he hounded the Christians, commanding all his subjects either to burn incense to the demons or, if they refused, to be condemned to death, and before their end to suffer many outrages over the whole body. Then, at that very moment, the blessed men made the tyrant's cruelty and the God-hating law an occasion for their own valour. They broke away from the other soldiers and formed a select, Christ-loving phalanx under the command of the power of the Spirit. They openly set themselves against the foul edicts, and all in harmony, as though with one tongue, they cried out our faith, saying that they cared little for this passing life and gave their bodies up to every form of punishment. The servant of that violent law, more tyrannical than the law itself, learned of the saints' resistance. He hastened to contrive a punishment to match their zeal, devising a new and unheard-of terror for souls that would not yield. 'If I threaten them with the sword,' he says, 'the fear is too small to cow them, and they will never submit. These are men who have lived under arms from boyhood and are used to bearing steel. If I bring other punishments against them, they will endure nobly, for they are no strangers to blows and wounds. Nor is fire fearful to men as resolutely set as these. So I must find a punishment whose action is painful and whose duration is long and drawn out.' What, then, did this sophist of evil carefully plot against the saints? After pondering,

he found a danger in the very air, which the season and the country readily supplied. The season was winter, and the place was Armenia, the neighbouring country, which, as you know, has a harsh winter. Not even in summer does it give its inhabitants warmth; it is warmed only just enough to ripen the ear of grain. The vine is not even known among them. Anyone who has not travelled far has never seen a bunch of grapes, and he asks about grapes as we ask about things that happen among the Indians. There the sower cuts the earth while snow is still lying, and snow overtakes the harvest. The winds strip the reaper unless he binds his clothes tightly about him and fights against the force of the blasts. Autumn and spring hardly exist there, for winter, a bad neighbour, drags them under its own dominion. In that country, then, and in the present month, he stripped the saints and stood them in the open with their bodies completely naked. He punished the disciples of piety in the opposite way to the king of the Assyrians with his Babylonian furnace. For pain, nothing compares with blazing fire and with frost that congeals and withers. Fire is like the sword and brings death swiftly; frost brings equal pain but draws out the end. In general, the afflictions caused by cold are slower: quartan fevers, cancers, carbuncles, and all the things the physicians in their learned theories declare that cold matter produces in bodies. So people of a colder and fattier constitution are more sluggish and have unwieldy bodies, and the same is true of the irrational animals. The warmer ones are swift and nimble when need presses; those of the opposite kind are slow and fettered by torpor. Thus the horse is swift, roused to the race by a whistle before the whip; the donkey is slow and barely finishes its journey under the cudgel. The leopard is quick, flying through the glens with its dry, hot body; the bear, on the contrary, with its heavier limbs, is sluggish. I have not lectured you on natural science out of season, but so that by examining the manner of the punishment you may learn the endurance of these men. Winter makes rivers that carry ships passable on foot, and turns flowing water into the hardness of stone. It splits rocks when it reaches deep into them. It harms opposite kinds of bodies equally, turning soft things to stone and breaking hard things apart. So wine, when it freezes, takes the shape of the jar that holds it, and soft oil stands solid, moulded to the space of its vessel, while glass and earthenware burst around their liquids and shatter. Of the animals whose lot is life on the mountains and in the open, some perish, while others, in the extremity of their distress, forget even their wildness. Deer and gazelles shelter in the folds, neither fearing the dogs then nor fleeing from those who come near. For a greater terror always drives out the timidity caused by lesser fears.

Birds come to dwell with people and stay under their roofs. People dig into the sea and cut the water with stonemasons' tools, and neighbours do not visit one another. Such a season became the tyrant's weapon against the martyrs. It was fitting, it seems, that the great and harmonious phalanx of the blessed should do battle under a new kind of punishment, so that they might win a glory for piety beyond comparison with the many other martyrs. So they stood there. Their limbs froze as they shivered, but they kept their resolve unshaken, and they offered a spectacle of contest to angels, to men and to demons. The angels awaited the parting of their souls, so that they might receive them and carry them up to their proper inheritance. The men eagerly awaited the outcome, testing the strength of our common nature: whether, through fear and hope of what is to come, we are able to overcome such great pains. The demons watched closely what was happening, longing to see the athletes fall and give up like cowards in the face of danger. But their hope was put to shame, because of God who gave the martyrs strength. For they saw the loss of their extremities, each his own and all of them one another's. One lay there with his foot or his fingers dropped away; another lay with his innate warmth chilled to the last. The most violent winds blow upon a thickly planted spot, shake its tall trees and bring them down to the earth roots and all. In the same way the winter laid low the ranks of the blessed: the noble plants of paradise, the glory of our race, the roots from which we ourselves have sprung, the soldiers of Paul, the bodyguards of Christ, the destroyers of altars, the builders of churches. They had enlisted to fight against barbarians, and they fought out their contest against the common enemy of humankind.

[?] and while fasting he flourished, and though he went without food he was better fleshed than those who lived in luxury. For this is God's special gift: in their straits he grants his faithful servants things beyond their hope. But since envy is always fixed close beside things that are lofty, the blessed company was in danger of being mutilated, and we very nearly lost the full number of the fourth ten. For one man gave up because of the cold at the very moment of victory. Alas! He abandoned his fellow soldiers and, through the tyrant's contrivance, went over to the bath. This lover of life sought to spare flesh that had already withered. But he lost his hope, and he did not gain even this passing life, for he died at once upon his transgression. He was a wretched Judas among the martyrs, neither a disciple nor rich, and yet he drew the noose upon himself. Let no one be surprised. This kind of trickery is the devil's habit against those who submit to him. He deceives and flatters in all sorts of ways in order to throw a man down; and once he has thrown him down, he immediately tramples on him and mocks him as he lies there. He makes merry over the disaster by adding disgrace to it, and he delights in the disgrace of the one he has lured. That is why the Psalmist called him 'enemy and avenger', showing his double-dealing character by the contradiction between the two names. He never becomes a friend of men or keeps faith with them; he only plays the friend when he wants to put on the mask of deceit. But he who comes to the aid of our weakness, who cultivates good things, good words and good deeds, found for himself, as with Abraham, a sheep for the sacrifice. He found a friend among those who were fighting them, a confessor among those who blasphemed, and a martyr from the ranks of the persecutors. One of the tyranny's executioners was granted a vision of the angels who came to the martyrs. He was bathed in light by the appearance of the holy spirits, as Paul once was by the glory of Christ when he was on his way to Damascus. At once he changed his mind, stripped off his clothes, and joined those who were freezing. In one brief moment he combined everything and became a convert, a confessor and a martyr, washed in his own blood with the bath of regeneration, blood that was deadened and did not flow. A man who won the crown, a man worthy of everything! Because of him I have the forty for the Church of God. Because of that noble man the ranks of the martyrs are not mutilated. Because of the convert we celebrate a complete festival with a complete number. And the devil suffered something delightful and laughable: while he was stealing a soldier, he was robbed of a persecutor and executioner. And what came after this? The thrice-blessed ones departed to the place they longed for. But the master of the punishment could not bear the martyrs' victory patiently, and he made war on their dead bodies. He ordered the dwellings of those holy souls to be given to the fire, and by this one act he imitated both savage beasts and bitter men. For the

[?] of persecuted people who have fled [?] to live [?] when [?] have withdrawn, they set fire to their houses [?] they destroy. And one of the martyrs might rightly have said to him: 'Vain man, I no longer fear your [?]. I was afraid, as long as [?] souls [?] to those who were freezing, that the excess of torture might [overcome?] the courage of the faithful. But now that this fear [is past?], use the clay that remains [as you please?] [?]. For the more you show your cruelty raging, the more you crown the victory of those who have departed. The fierce assaults of their opponents are exact proofs of the courage of those who prevailed.'

But why do we linger so long? The bodies were burned, and the fire took them over. The world divided that dust and the remains of the furnace among itself, and almost every land is blessed by these holy relics. I too have a share of the gift, and I have laid the bodies of my parents beside the relics of these soldiers, so that at the time of the resurrection they may be raised together with helpers who have great freedom of speech before God. For I know that they have power, and I have seen clear proofs of their boldness before God. Indeed, I want to tell you one of the things that bear wonderful witness to what they can do. Near the village that belongs to me, where the relics of these thrice-blessed men rest, there is a small neighbouring town called Ibora. A detachment of soldiers was stationed there, as is usual among the Romans, and one of the soldiers came to the village I mentioned. His commanding officer had assigned him to guard the place and to hold back the impulses and outrages of his fellow soldiers, which men under arms are accustomed to inflict on country people out of insolence. He was ailing in one of his feet and was lame, and the complaint was chronic and hard to cure. He went into the martyrs' shrine, where the saints rest, prayed to God and called on the saints to intercede. At night a man of dignified appearance appeared to him. After saying some other things, he said, 'You are lame, soldier, and need healing? Let me feel your foot.' In the dream he took hold of the foot and pulled hard. While the night vision did this, in waking reality there was such a crack as would happen if a bone slipped out of its natural joint and was then forcibly set back. It woke both those sleeping beside him and the soldier himself. The man got up at once and walked soundly, as he naturally used to. I saw this miracle myself, for I met the man as he was announcing it to everyone, proclaiming the martyrs' kindness and singing the praises of the soldiers' goodness. If I must add something that concerns me personally, I will tell it. When we were about to celebrate the first festival for the relics and lay the coffin to rest in the holy shrine, my mother

—for she was the one who gathered the people for God and arranged the feast—told me to come and take part in the proceedings. I was living far away at the time, still young and counted among the laity. As tends to happen when business is pressing, I was busy, and I foolishly took the summons with some resentment. I found fault with my mother for not putting the festival off to another time, but dragging me away from many cares to attend it, and with only one day's notice before the gathering. I arrived at the place. An all-night vigil was being held in a garden, where the relics of the saints were being honoured with the singing of psalms, and as I slept nearby in a small room, I saw a vision in a dream, as follows. I seemed to want to go into the garden where, in waking reality, the vigil was being held. When I reached the door, I saw a crowd of soldiers sitting at the entrance. All of a sudden they all stood up, raised their rods, rushed at me threateningly and would not let me in. I would even have been beaten, had not one of them, kinder than the rest as it seemed to me, begged me off. When sleep left me and I came to reflect on my fault over the summons, I realized what the frightening vision of the soldiers meant. I lamented my own folly with many tears, and over the very casket of the relics I shed bitter tears, so that God might be gracious to me and the holy soldiers grant me pardon. I have told these things so that we may be convinced that the martyrs are alive and are God's bodyguards and counsellors, they who today have benefited and adorned our Church. Brighter and greater is this Forty Days' fast, which holds the memory of the forty martyrs; the month is more illustrious than the other months; and the harsh winter no longer seems hard to me. I do not complain against the savagery of the present season, for it became the persecutor's weapon and so perfected this sacred phalanx for me. The mother of the seven Maccabees had a soul that loved God rather than the flesh. She did not blame the cruelty of Antiochus, the tyrant of Syria, nor was she distressed by the punishments and sufferings of her sons. She accepted her bereavement as a benefit, and the loss of her children as a help. Nor did Stephen, while he was being stoned, think he was being harmed; he thought rather that he was being given life. In the same way we too owe thanks to those who fought against God for the good outcome, since they became for us the cause of such great blessings, even though they acted not with the aim of benefactors but of enemies. For even enemies confer benefits without meaning to, benefits no less honourable than those of true friends. The devil helped Job more than he harmed him. The king of the Assyrians became Daniel's benefactor. Let the three young men give thanks to the furnace; let Isaiah, who was sawn in two, sing the praises of the Hebrews; let Zechariah, slain between the temple and the altar, honour his murderers; let John, who was beheaded, proclaim Herod a benefactor; let the apostles proclaim those who bound and scourged them; and let all the martyrs love

their persecutors. For if those men had not opened the stadium, the athletes would not have shown their courage to the world. What would one admire most in the men set before us for praise: their number, their courage, or their unfeigned harmony? First, let us not pass over their number without feeling or gratitude. Whoever has so many intercessors will never come away from prayer and petition with nothing achieved, even if he is heavily weighed down by sins. God himself is witness to this thought and hope, in his conversation with Abraham, when he accepted the plea for the people of Sodom. He sought not forty righteous men but ten, to spare a city that was about to be wiped out. And we, as the Apostle says, have so great a cloud of witnesses surrounding us. Let us count ourselves blessed, rejoicing in hope, persevering in prayer, and sharing in the commemorations of the saints. Forty martyrs are strong shield-bearers against our enemies and trustworthy advocates when we make supplication to the Master. With hope in them, let the Christian take courage when the devil stitches together temptations, when wicked men rise up, when tyrants seethe with anger, when the sea rages, when the earth fails to bear what it is appointed to produce for people, and when heaven threatens disaster. Their power is sufficient for every need and every circumstance, and it receives rich grace from Christ, to whom all glory is fitting for ever. Amen.
